2.text: hunters who are most successful in trapping are reputed by the Russianized

3.text: natives to have bought their luck from the “master” of the forest with

4.text: brandy and packs of cards. The “masters” of forests are constantly playing

5.text: cards with one another. The stake is some species of game, which may

6.text: then have to pass from one to another after the play is over. This

7.text: accounts for the migrations of game. N. Dyachkoff, whose book has already

10.text: The “master” of the river has very white thick skin. His wife has

11.text: remarkably long hair, which floats around her on the water. Whoever sees

12.text: her, or hears her loud, piercing cry, goes raving mad. The “master” of the

13.text: forest hunts the “master” of the river in order to obtain his skin, of which

14.text: he makes for himself the “magic” boots (in local Russian, четвери, “fourfold”).
14.note: Pre-reform Russian check per keying_spec.md §2.7: четвери contains none of the five obsolete sorts (і ѣ ѳ ѵ, word-final ъ); keyed as printed.

15.text: These are the well-known “four-leagued” boots of the fairy-tales of the

16.text: civilized world, which enable their wearers to make four miles at every step.

17.text: The “master” of the river retaliates by catching the feet of the “master” of

18.text: the forest, or those of members of his family who happen to cross the river

19.text: upon the ice. Once, when the “master” of the forest and his pregnant wife

20.text: were running a race on the ice of the Kolyma River, near the cliffs of

21.text: Khandgiboy, the “master” of the river caught the wife by the feet, and

22.text: dragged her down into the water. Her husband, with the assistance of his

23.text: brother, tried to pull her out, but they succeeded only in tearing off her

24.text: head. They placed this on the top of Khandgiboy, where it may still be

26.text: The “master” of the river or the “owner” of the lake does not like iron

27.text: tools. When an axe or an ice-pick is accidentally dropped into the water,

28.text: the “master” gets angry, and stops the supply of fish for several years. In

29.text: the same way, these “masters” are also very jealous concerning ancient

30.text: customs connected with hunting and fishing. Both the Chukchee and the

31.text: Russianized natives, when they go to a new place for a protracted stay,

32.text: offer a little sacrifice to the “master” of the place, especially if they intend

33.text: to hunt or fish in his dominions. Otherwise he would appear to them in

34.text: their sleep, and demand the sacrifice. The best material for this sacrifice is

35.text: tobacco. On the whole, the natives in many cases prefer to sacrifice im-

36.text: ported provisions, Russian or American, supposing that the local “masters”

37.text: and deities need them much more than ordinary food, which is abundant.

38.text: The Russianized natives, as well as the Chukchee, often call the “master”

39.text: of the place simply “the old man.”
